claims.text: Introducing nanoscale Y2O3 dispersoids into a W-Ta-Mo-Nb-based refractory high-entropy alloy will strengthen it at high temperatures.
The oxide-dispersed alloy will retain the refractory HEA's inherent thermal stability.
The oxide-dispersed alloy will retain the refractory HEA's inherent irradiation stability.
Mechanical alloying followed by spark plasma sintering can incorporate approximately 2–3 vol% nanoscale Y2O3 into the alloy matrix.
The proposed powder-metallurgy route will produce a uniform dispersion of Y2O3 nanoparticles.
Uniformly dispersed Y2O3 nanoparticles will refine the grain size.
Uniformly dispersed Y2O3 nanoparticles will pin grain boundaries.
Uniformly dispersed Y2O3 nanoparticles will obstruct dislocation motion.
Impeded dislocation motion will provide dispersion strengthening.
The oxide dispersoids will stabilize the alloy microstructure at high temperature.
Relative to an alloy without oxide dispersoids, the oxide-dispersed alloy will have higher yield strength at approximately 1000–1200°C.
Relative to an alloy without oxide dispersoids, the oxide-dispersed alloy will have improved creep resistance at approximately 1000–1200°C.
The oxide-dispersed alloy will have thermal stability comparable to the baseline alloy.
The oxide-dispersed alloy will have irradiation stability comparable to the baseline alloy under reactor-relevant simulated irradiation.
An oxide concentration above an unspecified optimum may embrittle or otherwise degrade the alloy.
The magnitude of strengthening and the optimal dispersoid concentration depend on processing parameters and Y2O3 volume fraction.
Failure to obtain a statistically significant improvement in yield strength and creep resistance while retaining similar thermal and irradiation stability would falsify the hypothesis.
